analysis.one_liner: Requires big freight railroads to staff main-line trains with a two-person crew.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Safe Freight Act would have written into law that big freight railroads (Class I carriers) cannot run a main-line freight train with a single crew member: every such train would need both a certified conductor and a certified engineer. It includes exceptions for low-risk moves like yard switching, but not for the most dangerous trains carrying flammable, toxic, or explosive cargo, and not for very long trains. It died without any action in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Railroad workers, especially conductors and engineers, gain a statutory floor on crew staffing and preserved jobs; the public gains a second trained crew member on trains carrying flammable, toxic, or explosive cargo.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Rail workers and communities near rail lines

how_it_helps.text: Requires Class I freight railroads to staff main-line freight trains with both a certified conductor and a certified engineer.
Applies regardless of train length or cargo for long trains and high-hazard trains, closing the gaps that would let the most dangerous trains run with one person.

analysis.who_pays: Class I freight railroads bear the cost of staffing every covered main-line train with a second crew member; those costs are absorbed by railroad shareholders or passed into shipping prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathers any operations already running with one-person crews for at least a year before enactment, so it does not force railroads to undo existing one-person operations unless the Transportation Secretary finds they are not equivalently safe.

Railroads could obtain waivers from the two-person requirement, and many low-speed or non-main-line operations are exempt, so the practical reach of the mandate is narrower than a full crew-size floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is real: crewed trains are the last line of defense on trains carrying hazardous cargo, and the cost of crewing is small relative to railroad profits. The main drawback is that grandfathing existing one-person operations and the waiver provision blunt how much change the bill would actually force; most new trains would be covered, but the railroads' current practice could largely continue under existing operations and waivers. A stronger version would have closed those doors.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Railroads subcommittee, and no vote or hearing ever happened before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 18, 2024, with one Republican cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials the next day.
No further action was taken; the bill died in subcommittee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It attracted only one cosponsor, so it lacked the support needed to move.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large freight railroads, which avoid a two-person crew mandate and the labor cost it carries.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.

for.name: Rep. Michael Rulli
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor, giving it modest bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.what_they_did: Oppose federal crew-size mandates, which would raise the cost of running trains with fewer crew members.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but never advanced far enough for a party-line test.

industries.note: The bill would raise labor costs by mandating two crew members on main-line trains, and railroads have for years sought to cut crew sizes. Their interest runs against a safety rule the public bears the risk of.

industries.industry: Rail labor unions and rail workers
industries.note: The bill preserves conductor and engineer jobs and codifies staffing levels that collective bargaining has not secured.
